title: Southwell Minster
tagline: The Cathedral & Parish Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary — a Norman jewel of the English Midlands, in continuous prayer since 627.

history.heading: A brief history
history.lede: A minster church has stood at Southwell for well over a thousand years — outlasting Vikings, the Reformation, civil war and fire — and today serves as the mother church of the Diocese of Southwell & Nottingham.
paragraphs: Tradition holds that Paulinus, the first Archbishop of York, founded the earliest church here in 627 while baptising converts in the River Trent. In 956 King Eadwig granted land at Southwell to Oskytel, Archbishop of York, and a Saxon minster church was established; the manor was recorded in detail in the Domesday Book of 1086.

The present Norman Minster was begun about 1108, rebuilt over the earlier Anglo-Saxon foundations. The nave, transepts, central tower and the two western “pepperpot” towers survive as one of the finest examples of severe Romanesque design in England. The Early English quire was rebuilt between 1234 and 1251, and the celebrated Chapter House was begun in 1288.

Suppressed by Henry VIII in 1540, the collegiate church was refounded in 1543, lost its status again in 1548, and was finally restored in 1557. During the Civil War, Charles I surrendered at Southwell in 1646 after the siege of Newark. In 1711 lightning struck the south-west spire and fire destroyed the roofs, bells, clock and organ; both spires were removed in 1805 and only rebuilt in 1879–81 during Ewan Christian’s extensive Victorian restoration.

The Minster became a cathedral in 1884, when the new Diocese of Southwell was created to serve Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire (Derby becoming a separate diocese in 1927). It remains dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and, uniquely among English cathedrals, retains its ancient title of Minster.

history.figureCaption: The Norman west front, with its distinctive “pepperpot” towers and the 1996 Angel Window by Patrick Reyntiens.

timeline.text: Paulinus, first Archbishop of York, credited with founding a church at Southwell.
King Eadwig grants land to Archbishop Oskytel; a Saxon minster is established.
Norman rebuilding begins at the east end; nave commenced after 1120.
The Early English quire is rebuilt.
Construction of the octagonal Chapter House begins.
The great stone pulpitum (choir screen) is carved in the Decorated style.
Suppressed under Henry VIII, restored under Philip and Mary.
Charles I surrenders to Scottish Presbyterian troops at Southwell.
Lightning strike; fire destroys the roofs, bells, clock and organ.
Ewan Christian’s restoration; the western spires are re-erected.
Southwell Minster becomes a cathedral of the new diocese.
Patrick Reyntiens’ great Angel Window installed at the west end.
Chapter House reopens after major restoration, with cantilever lift for full access.

treasures.heading: Treasures and places of interest
treasures.lede: From England’s finest medieval leaf-carvings to a 16th-century Flemish east window, the Minster is unusually rich in things worth pausing over.
treasures.leavesBody: The Chapter House (begun 1288) is octagonal, has no central pillar, and is decorated with the deeply-undercut foliage carvings collectively known as “The Leaves of Southwell.” Individual species — ivy, maple, oak, hop, hawthorn — are all identifiable, interspersed with Green Men and mythological figures. Regarded as the finest 13th-century naturalistic carving in the United Kingdom, they were the subject of Nikolaus Pevsner’s classic 1945 monograph and were voted Britain’s favourite cathedral treasure in a 2023 public poll.
treasures.figureAlt: Naturalistic 13th-century leaf carvings around the doorway of Southwell Minster’s Chapter House.
treasures.figureCaption: “The Leaves of Southwell” — 13th-century foliage carvings around the Chapter House portal, voted the nation’s favourite cathedral treasure in 2023.

features.heading: The Norman nave
features.body: Seven bays of short, circular columns with scalloped capitals; a single large triforium arch in each bay; small round-headed clerestory windows and circular external openings — one of the outstanding survivals of severe English Romanesque.

features.heading: The tympanum
features.body: The late-11th-century carved tympanum in the north transept, together with a fragment of tessellated floor, are the sole visible remains of the earlier Anglo-Saxon minster.

features.heading: The pulpitum (rood screen)
features.body: An elaborately carved stone choir screen of 1320–40, an outstanding example of the Decorated style, with two storeys of ogee-arched niches and openwork gables framing the entrance to the quire.

features.heading: The Early English quire
features.body: Rebuilt 1234–51 in a pure Early English style: clustered columns, twin lancets to the upper storey, ribbed stone vault and a square east end lit by two tiers of four lancet windows.

features.heading: The east window
features.body: Four Renaissance panels of 16th-century Flemish glass by Jean Chastellain, after designs by Noël Bellemare, originally made for the Temple Church in Paris and presented to the Minster in 1818; the four evangelists above are by Clayton & Bell (1876).

features.heading: The Angel Window
features.body: Installed at the west end in 1996, this great modern window by Patrick Reyntiens — one of Britain’s foremost stained-glass artists — is the Minster’s most striking recent addition.

features.heading: Tomb of Archbishop Sandys
features.body: The finest of the Minster’s memorials: the alabaster tomb of Edwin Sandys, Archbishop of York (d. 1588), whose family long held estates in Nottinghamshire.

features.heading: The Newstead lectern
features.body: A medieval brass eagle lectern, believed to have been recovered from the lake at Newstead Abbey after the Dissolution and given to the Minster by Archdeacon Kaye in 1805.

features.heading: The central Norman tower
features.body: Two ornamental stages — intersecting arches below, plain arches above — place the crossing tower high among England’s surviving Norman towers.

features.heading: Chapels for prayer
features.body: Three chapels are set aside for private prayer, including St Oswald’s Chapel (used daily for Morning Prayer and Holy Communion) and the Airmen’s Chapel, commemorating RAF Bomber Command in Nottinghamshire.

officers.heading: Principal officers
officers.lede: Southwell Minster is governed by its Chapter, chaired by the Dean, with support and oversight from the Cathedral Council and the wider College of Canons. Below are the principal office-holders as currently listed by the Minster.

people.name: The Very Revd Dr Stephen Evans
The Revd Canon Dr Richard Frith
The Revd Canon Dr Stephen Hippisley-Cox

officers.note: The Non-Executive members of Chapter also include Mr Andrew Corner, Mr Nick Alexander, Mrs Ann Carter-Gray, Mrs Marion Oswald, Mr David Walker and Mr Jonathan Wheeler. The Cathedral also employs a Chief Operating Officer and Chief Finance Officer alongside some 32 staff and around 300 volunteers.

music.heading: Music foundation & choirs
music.lede: A choir has sung at Southwell for more than nine hundred years — a continuous tradition of choral worship stretching from the medieval Vicars Choral to today's Cathedral Choir of boy and girl choristers, professional Lay Clerks and the volunteer Minster Chorale.
songParagraphs: The Minster's musical life began with a college of Vicars Choral, resident in the buildings that stood on the site of today's Vicars' Court. One or two of their number were designated Rector Chori — “Ruler of the Choir” — a title first formally recorded at Southwell in 1499 and still used for the Director of Music today. Boy Choristers were added to the Vicars Choral, and the Vicars were gradually replaced by lay singers — the Lay Clerks — giving the choir substantially the shape it has today.

In 2005 a Girls’ Choir was founded by the then Assistant Director of Music. It was fully integrated into the Cathedral Choir in 2019; today boy and girl choristers enjoy complete parity, sharing services, robes (cassock and surplice), age ranges and title — all are simply Cathedral Choristers. In 2021 Southwell appointed its first-ever female head chorister in the Minster’s thousand-year history, and in 2025 the Minster celebrated the Girls’ Choir’s twentieth anniversary.
music.figureAlt: The medieval stone pulpitum of Southwell Minster with the Nicholson organ mounted above.
music.figureCaption: The pulpitum with the main Nicholson organ mounted above, in its Caröe case.

features.heading: Boy Choristers
features.body: The traditional treble line, drawn from The Minster School. The boys usually sing on their own for Monday and Tuesday Evensong and join the Lay Clerks from Thursday to Sunday during term, alternating with the girls.

features.heading: Girl Choristers
features.body: Founded in 2005 and now fully equal partners in the Cathedral Choir — currently around 18 girls, sharing all chorister duties, rehearsals, tours and recordings on the same footing as the boys.

features.heading: Lay Clerks
features.body: Six professional Lay Clerks and six Auxiliary Lay Clerks — the adult alto, tenor and bass lines, direct descendants of the medieval Vicars Choral. They sing with the choristers from Thursday to Sunday and on feast days.

features.heading: The Minster Chorale
features.body: Founded in 1994, an auditioned adult voluntary choir of up to thirty singers directed by the Assistant Director of Music. Sings for services when the Cathedral Choir is on leave, plus monthly Sunday Mattins.

features.heading: The Minster School
features.body: All choristers are educated at The Minster School, a Church of England academy with a music-specialist Junior Department (Years 3–6) and a member of the Choir Schools’ Association.

features.heading: Southwell Choral Society
features.body: A non-auditioning community choir of over sixty years’ standing, rehearsing weekly in the Minster during term — the wider musical community that gathers around the foundation.

music.organsBody: The Minster’s main instrument stands on the medieval pulpitum in an oak case designed by W. D. Caröe. The present Screen Organ was rebuilt through the 1990s by leading organ builders (advised by John Norman, Stephen Bicknell and Ian Bell) with the Caröe case preserved on historical grounds. A separate Nave Organ, whose lineage traces back to a 1662 instrument by “Mr Derbie” and repairs after the great fire of 1711, supports congregational singing at the west end, and a fine chamber organ is used for continuo and smaller-scale liturgy. A 72-page illustrated booklet, The Organs of Southwell Minster by former Rector Chori Paul Hale, is available from the Cathedral Shop.

worship.heading: Liturgy and daily services
worship.lede: The Minster’s daily round of prayer follows the Church of England’s Common Worship pattern, sustained during term by one of the country’s most distinguished cathedral music foundations.
paragraphs: Southwell keeps a full Anglican cathedral daily office: Morning Prayer, Holy Communion (the Eucharist) and Evening Prayer or Evensong are offered every day. Choral services are sung most days during school terms by the Cathedral Choir — the Boy Choristers, Girl Choristers and Lay Clerks — who between them provide music for eight choral services a week. On Sundays the Girl and Boy Choristers sing the Eucharist and Evensong in rotation with the Lay Clerks. Additional services are sung by the Minster Chorale, a chamber choir of up to thirty volunteer singers founded in 1994.

The Sunday Cathedral Eucharist (10.00am) and Sunday Evensong (3.30pm) are live-streamed and remain available online for a week and a day respectively. Visitors of all traditions are warmly welcome; there is no admission charge.

worship.figureCaption: The Early English quire, where choral Evensong is sung most days during term.

visit.heading: Opening hours
visit.lede: The Minster is open to visitors every day of the year, without charge. Donations towards its upkeep are gratefully received.

cards.heading: The Cathedral
cards.note: Stewards are normally on duty from 10.30am to 5.00pm (Mon–Sat) and 11.00am to 5.00pm on Sunday. Occasional service or event closures may apply at short notice.

cards.heading: Minster Office
cards.note: The Minster Centre houses the office, education team and tourist information point.

cards.heading: Archbishop’s Palace & Gardens
cards.note: Free entry to the ruined medieval palace and sensory gardens adjoining the Minster.

donate.heading: Donate
paragraphs: The stone above you was raised in eleven hundred and eight. It is the finest Norman nave left standing in England — round arch after round arch, cut by men who knew they would never live to see the roof closed over them.

And walk east, into the Chapter House. There, carved into the stone eight hundred years ago, are the leaves of this county. Hawthorn; oak; maple; buttercup, and vine. Whoever cut them had clearly walked out into the woods and looked — really looked — at a living thing, and made it permanent. They have not withered in seven centuries.
None of this is a museum. It is an active place of worship, still worked, still sung in, still lit; a place of spiritual warmth and comfort.
It costs more than five thousand pounds a day simply to keep these doors open — the heating, the glass, the fabric, the choristers, the liturgy.

There is no charge to come in. There never has been, and the Chapter will keep it that way. You can, however, play an important part in helping with this mission. Last year the average visitor left one pound and eighty-eight pence.
We'd like to ask you for a donation of five pounds.

If this place has given you a moment of stillness today, and enriched your day, please give it your help — by using the “Donate now” button: tick Gift Aid if you're a UK taxpayer: for each £5 it adds an extra £1.25, and it costs you nothing extra.
donate.after: Most importantly please recognise that you leave this place with no obligation. Please only give according to your means. Do not give what you can ill-afford. You leave always with the Lord's blessing.
donate.close: The leaves have lasted eight hundred years. Whether they last another eight hundred is, rather quietly, up to us.

contact.heading: Contact & how to find us
gettingHere: Southwell is a small market town in central Nottinghamshire, seven miles from the A1 and about 30 minutes by road from Nottingham on the A612. The Minster stands on Church Street in the centre of the town, a short walk from the Saturday market square.
Guided tours can be pre-booked through the Minster Office; education visits are arranged separately on 01636 817287.
Online worship: the Sunday Eucharist and Evensong are live-streamed from the Minster’s website and remain available for catch-up during the following week.
